ios.desc:
Local Hours is a local-first time tracking app for iPhone and iPad. Track your work with widgets and quick actions, generate clean timesheets, and email approvers—without accounts, servers, or data lock-in.

- Track from anywhere
Start and stop a simple timer using home screen widgets, lock screen widgets, or the app itself. Add a short description when you stop so you remember what you worked on.
- Folder-based storage
All of your data lives as plain JSON files in a folder you choose. Back it up, sync it with iCloud, Dropbox, or another provider, or move it to a new device—it's just files.
- Automatic timesheets
Generate weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly timesheets from your entries. See total hours, per-day breakdowns, and a clear summary before you send anything.
- Email-ready exports
Create an email draft with an embedded timesheet summary and optional CSV attachment. Quickly send your hours to managers, clients, or payroll without copying and pasting.
- Smart reminders
Configure when you want to be reminded (for example, Friday at 5pm) and Local Hours prompts you to send your latest timesheet so you don't forget.
- Cross-device friendly format
The storage format is shared with the Mac version and future platforms. Point both apps at the same cloud folder and your data stays in sync across all your devices.
- Privacy by design
No analytics, no tracking, and no online account. Everything stays on your device unless you choose to sync the folder via your own tools.
Local Hours is open source, MIT licensed, and built for people who prefer simple tools that respect their data.

quotes.text:
Have you clocked in yet?

I built Local Hours, a simple time tracking / timesheet app that treats your data as plain files instead of rows in someone else’s database.

No accounts, no backend – All time entries and timesheets are JSON files in a folder you pick. Sync happens via iCloud / Dropbox / OneDrive if you want it.

Cross-device by design – The macOS menu bar app and iOS app both point at the same folder, so they “sync” via your storage provider without any server code.

Timesheets, not dashboards – The main job is: track time, then generate a weekly/bi-weekly/monthly timesheet you can actually send to an approver.

Exports that don’t trap you – You can send an email with an embedded summary + CSV, or just open the JSON files yourself.

Privacy – No analytics, no telemetry, no in-app purchases. It’s MIT-licensed and fully open source.

Apps are free on the App Store (iPhone, iPad, Mac):
https://apps.apple.com/us/app/local-hours-simple-timesheet/id6758984365

Repo (code, storage format, docs, screenshots):
https://github.com/gogrinimish/LocalHours

I’d especially like feedback on:
Does the “just files” approach line up with how you’d want to archive or script your own timesheets?
Is the UX for picking the storage folder and sharing it across devices clear enough?
What’s missing for you to actually use this for client work?

quotes.text:
I built Local Hours because I needed a simple time tracker that doesn't require online accounts, send data to someone else's cloud, and lock me into proprietary formats.

Local Hours stores everything as plain JSON files in a folder you choose. Point it at an iCloud, Google Drive, or OneDrive folder and your data syncs across devices automatically — no docker, no backend, no accounts, no analytics.

How it works:
- Start/stop a timer from the macOS menu bar or iOS widgets
- Add a short description when you stop
- Generate weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly timesheets
- Email approvers with an embedded summary or CSV attachment

The storage format is intentionally simple so you can inspect, back up, or migrate your data anytime. Both the macOS and iOS apps point at the same folder, so cross-device sync just works via your cloud storage provider.

It's free on the App Store (iPhone, iPad, Mac): https://apps.apple.com/us/app/local-hours-simple-timesheet/id6758984365

Built with Swift/SwiftUI. MIT licensed. No tracking, no telemetry, no in-app purchases.

I'd love feedback on the UX, the local-first approach, or ideas for what to build next. Android is planned.
